query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In steels operating in corrosive, high‐temperature environments, increasing the concentration of strong oxide-forming elements (e.g., aluminum) promotes the rapid in-situ formation of a continuous, dense alumina (Al2O3) scale that acts as a diffusion barrier to both oxygen ingress and metal ion dissolution, thereby enhancing the corrosion resistance of the steel.
generation.material_initial_state: A ferritic/martensitic steel (e.g., a T91-type steel) with a conventional low-Al content and typical microstructure that forms discontinuous or less protective oxide layers at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by increasing the aluminum (and possibly optimizing silicon) content, and/or adjust the oxygen content in the corrosive medium to promote in-situ alumina formation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature environments (e.g., 550–600 °C) in liquid metal systems (such as lead or lead-bismuth eutectic) with controlled oxygen partial pressures similar to those in advanced nuclear or chemical-processing applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and continuity of a protective Al2O3 oxide film on the steel’s surface.
generation.mechanism: A higher Al content leads to a preferential oxidation reaction that forms a dense, thermodynamically stable alumina layer. This continuous film restricts further oxygen ingress as well as outward diffusion of reactive metal ions, thereby reducing the rate of dissolution corrosion and inhibiting secondary oxidation processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with increased aluminum content will develop a more uniform and continuous alumina scale and exhibit lower corrosion depths, mass loss, and improved electrochemical impedance parameters compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Steels with standard alloy compositions that form less-protective, discontinuous Fe- or Cr-rich oxide layers under identical high-temperature, liquid-metal corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under high-temperature (approximately 550–600 °C) liquid metal environments with controlled oxygen levels, typical of nuclear-reactor and chemical-processing applications. Its effectiveness may be limited when other corrosion modes (e.g., stress corrosion cracking or pitting initiated by inclusions) dominate or at temperatures significantly beyond the studied range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative threshold for the optimal aluminum (and synergistic silicon) content and the role of microstructural factors (such as grain size and dispersoid distribution) in the kinetics and stability of the alumina film remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel specimens: one with a standard (baseline) aluminum content and one with an increased aluminum content. Expose both sets to a simulated liquid lead or lead-bismuth eutectic environment maintained at 600 °C with a controlled oxygen concentration (e.g., ~10^(-6) wt%). Over predetermined exposure durations (e.g., 1000 to 2000 hours), periodically extract samples and analyze the surface oxide layer using SEM, EDS, and XRD; measure corrosion depth via cross-sectional optical microscopy; and perform electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).
measurements: Continuity, composition, and thickness of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Al specimens do not form a more continuous and protective Al2O3 scale, or if they do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in corrosion metrics (e.g., corrosion depth, mass loss, or improved impedance characteristics) compared to the baseline specimens, then the hypothesis that increased Al content enhances corrosion resistance via alumina scale formation will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Traditional steels will be severely corroded in a lead and/or LBE environment, especially when the temperature is higher than 500 °C. The high dissolution rate of the main elements of steel in liquid lead brings great hidden dangers to the safe service of the structure materials. One of the main approaches to fight lead corrosion is to form a protective layer on the surface of the materials by a reasonable control of the oxygen content in liquid lead []. For traditional steel, such as T91, Fe- and Cr-rich oxide layers will form during oxidation, but their structure is not dense enough to protect the matrix, especially at a high temperature. Forming a more stable and protective oxide layer on the surface of steel by optimizing the alloy design received more attention on the materials R&D of LFR in recent years. Al has a strong oxygen affinity; the standard Gibbs formation energy and required oxygen concentration of Al oxidation in lead is lower than those of the Fe, Cr, and Si elements, while the thermodynamic stability of the oxidation product Al2O3 is stronger. AbstractThe 9–12% Cr ferritic–martensitic heat-resistant steel is the main candidate structural material for the Lead-cooled Faster Reactor. The lower Gibbs free energy change of Si oxide can promote the formation of a stable oxide layer, which can improve the corrosion resistance of the material. Therefore, it is of great significance to study the effect of silicon (Si) on the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE). The corrosion resistance of T91 steel with Si contents of 0.5 wt.%, 1.3 wt.%, and 2.0 wt.%, both in dynamic and static LBE at 550 °C, was investigated. The microstructure was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM), while the oxide films were characterized by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). Results show that the addition of Si is conducive to improving the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in LBE. T91 steel with high Si content has a thinner and more stable oxide film. The change of Si content can change the contact angle between the steel and LBE, and the contact angle is the largest when the Si content is 1.3 wt.%.
